content.title: NCIS Episode 500 death explained interview
content.text: Once upon a time, CBS's long-running procedural NCIS regularly killed off characters. At the end of Season 2, for example, Sasha Alexander's Special Agent Caitlin Todd took a bullet to the head in a shocking moment that told audience members nobody was safe in this dangerous world. Since then, other characters have met untimely fates, but as NCIS hits the big 5-0-0 in its episode count, executive producer Steve Binder felt that a fresh death would keep the audience on the edge of their seat — and ensure that the procedural would live on for another 500 episodes. “I don't think it can be understated the amount of energy that infused into the series,” Binder tells Gold Derby of his decision to swing the scythe again. So which character ends up six feet under on "All Good Things," aka Episode 500? This time it's NCIS Director Leon Vance, who has been played by Rocky Carroll since the end of Season 5. And Binder says that the actor didn't fight his fate. “I brought it up to Rocky and he was on board," the executive producer recalls. "He's a team player and recognized the value of the story. I'd really hate for us to be surprised in a year or two that we're off the air, and we never got a chance to do this story. would be a super dramatic gut punch but in a way make people remember what they love about the show.” Gold Derby spoke with Carroll about Vance’s swan song — and how he’ll still be a part of the NCIS family forever even if it’s not in front of the camera. Rocky Carroll's Leon Vance is permanently retired in the show's 500th episodeRobert Voets/CBS Gold Derby: What was your conversation like with Steve Binder when you found out what was planned for the 500th episode? Rocky Carroll: It was a very surreal and kind of an out of body experience because Steve was a writer on the series when I started, and he's worked his way up the ladder and is now the executive producer. I've known him for a very long time. At the end of a typical workday, I get a knock on my trailer door, and Steve comes in. He goes, “We've got this great idea for the 500th episode of NCIS.” He starts to tell me that the agency is close to being dissolved and there’s this nefarious character who's doing all these things to sabotage the agency. But thanks to Director Vance, the agency is saved and in the process of saving the agency, Vance loses his life. He goes, “Do you want to hear more about it?” And I'm thinking to myself, “Well, let me process what you just told me.” I got the understanding of what it was and the understanding that it's the 500th episode so we want to do something that makes our viewers go, “Oh, my God, I can't believe what just happened!” Steve said: “As a credit to you, the character of director Leon Vance was always supposed to be a supporting character and was never supposed to be much of a significant character. Even when Don Bellisario [the show’s co-creator] wrote the role of NCIS director, it was never considered to be a major component to the show. But because of what you brought to the role, we couldn't stop writing for the character. And because of your chemistry with Mark Harmon, suddenly the director of NCIS became this very significant character.” He also said: “It's going to be a love letter to your character and to you and what you brought to this show for 18 years." Did you express any wishes that you had for your final episode? I knew Steve was writing it and I knew that it was important to him that this story be really special. I was completely confident in that. But the only thing more surprising than getting the news about was how quickly I was able to be at peace with it. When I read the script, I was like, “Oh, yeah, this is going to be a good episode.” Let’s talk about the fake out where we see Vance get shot, but believe he was wearing a bulletproof vest. Then we realize that was just his version of the story — what really happened was there was no bulletproof vest and Vance died. What did you make of that? It was really in line with what I loved about the story. With the interrogation that Vance goes through in the episode, you don't realize until the end that he's basically talking to the Angel of Death (played by Adhir Kalyan). And the angel is telling Vance, “You need to go back and put together the pieces, and then everything will be revealed to you.” That format was so great because in Vance's mind, [the bulletproof vest] is what happened. And then the Grim Reaper says, “No, that's not exactly how it went.” People will see touches of It's a Wonderful Life with Vance as Jimmy Stewart and he’s saying, “This is what happened to you, old pal.” How did you approach the moment where we see the recognition on Vance’s face as he realizes what's happened? Any actor worth his salt will tell you if it's on the page, it's a lot easier to do. Because the episode was so well-written, it was easy to get to that place. If I was doing this scene 20 or 25 years ago, it probably would have been much harder. But at this stage in your life, you've had a few experiences and you've dealt with death and all the things. It's like my acting teacher told me when I was 19 years old, “Most of what you're learning now will not resonate with you until you're older." Vance's swan song in 'NCIS' (Robert Voets/CBS) How was it to work with Adam Campbell as young Ducky? Adam had done episodes in the past, but it never involved my character, so we had never done any scenes together because they were always flashbacks. Whenever Adam would come on the show, I'd always see him in the hair and makeup trailer, but this was the first time we were actually in the scene together. What was that last day like on set? It was not as bittersweet because I knew that I'd be coming back to direct an episode a month later. It was not really “Goodbye” but “See you later.” I'm still a family member. I'm not going to be here for meals every night, but I'll still be here for Christmas and Thanksgiving, you know? In the moment, it was still that realization that this is the last time that we're going to be doing this. As an actor, you've been playing one character for 18 years. I think maybe only Susan Lucci and a handful of other people would know how that feels. What will you be doing the night the episode airs? I will be at a screening in New York City for SAG-AFTRA members who will be watching this for the first time, and then I'll do a Q&A once it ends. I have this image of the episode finishing, the house lights come up, and there's a room full of people with their mouths agape. What else do you want to be doing outside of the NCIS world? Will you take a breather? After 18 seasons, if you don't allow yourself to take a breather, shame on you! I imagine myself like the opening of The Mary Tyler Moore Show where you're just kind of walking around and you throw your hat up in the air. My running joke is I've never been jealous of anybody else's job or career, with the exception of people who travel around the world and get to eat and drink and immerse themselves in other people's culture. If I could do anything else, it would be along the lines of Anthony Bourdain, Tony Shalhoub, or Eva Longoria, where I would just travel the world, go on as many fishing boats as I can, and immerse myself in people's culture. Like Somebody Feed Phil on Netflix. We’ll call it Somebody Feed Rocky! There you go. I like it.
